clue.text: Gong finally sounded in the middle of Dinner for One

indicators.note: a letter placed in the middle of a word is enclosed by the rest of that word

parts.note: a dinner for one person is simply a meal; the phrase is also the title of a famous comedy sketch

indicators.note: 'finally' points to the last letter of the word it qualifies, 'sounded'

parts.note: last letter of 'sounded'

explanation.surface: A dinner gong rings out in the middle of the old New Year's Eve comedy sketch Dinner for One.
explanation.walkthrough: The gong looks like part of the dinner scene, but it is the definition. D sits in the middle of MEAL, splitting it ME-AL.
explanation.definitionFit: Gong is British slang for a medal or official award, especially one given by the state.

clue.text: Masculine energy surrounds Milan club

indicators.note: the letters from 'masculine energy' go around the letters from 'Milan'

parts.note: M is the grammar abbreviation for masculine
E is the physics symbol for energy
the football team is AC Milan

explanation.surface: A macho burst of energy surrounds the Milan football club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Milan club' reads as one football team, but the definition is 'club' alone and 'Milan' gives the AC of AC Milan.
explanation.definitionFit: A mace is a heavy spiked weapon, a type of club used in medieval battle.

clue.text: After taking counsel Dave gets discharged, set free

definitions.note: the answer is a past participle; 'after taking counsel' describes a decision already weighed

indicators.note: a word that is discharged is emptied of its contents, so only the outer letters of 'Dave' stay

parts.note: 'Dave' with its middle emptied
to set free is to liberate

explanation.surface: After talking to his lawyer, a prisoner called Dave is discharged and walks out of jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discharged' seems to be about Dave's release, but it empties his name to D-E; 'set free' then does the releasing.
explanation.definitionFit: A deliberated decision is one reached after careful thought and discussion, which is taking counsel.

clue.text: Most vulgar Suffolk resort often deserted

indicators.note: the resort's name is deserted by the word for 'often', which walks out of it

parts.note: Lowestoft is a seaside town on the Suffolk coast in eastern England
oft is the old word for often

explanation.surface: A crude seaside town in Suffolk is often empty of visitors.
explanation.walkthrough: Lowestoft, the most easterly town in Britain, loses its final OFT.
explanation.definitionFit: Low means coarse or common in taste, so the superlative describes the crudest or most vulgar.

clue.text: Directed UK films about old Conservative country for Americans

indicators.note: a film director arranges the material, so 'UK films' and the extra letters are put into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
O is the standard abbreviation for old
C is the abbreviation for the Conservative party

explanation.surface: Someone directed British films about an old Conservative politician, and the country is aimed at American audiences.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country' looks like a nation, but to Americans it is also a style of music. 'About' simply gathers the O and C into the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Americans loosely lump traditional rural songs together as country, a close cousin of the genre named here.

clue.text: Happy speciality? Catching marine fish

indicators.note: the word for 'speciality' catches the fish as a net would, holding it inside

parts.note: one's forte is one's strong point
the tuna is a large sea fish

explanation.surface: An angler is happy that their speciality is landing sea fish.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark after 'speciality' makes it look like a separate remark, but it is the container that swallows the fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Happy in its older sense means lucky, as in a happy chance, which is the answer's meaning.

clue.text: Record extremes of idealistic reasoning

parts.note: a log is a written record, as a ship's log

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two end letters, here of 'idealistic'

parts.note: first and last letters of 'idealistic'

explanation.surface: Someone notes down the most extreme examples of idealistic thinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremes' sounds like extreme views, but it means only the two ends of 'idealistic'.
explanation.definitionFit: Logic is the discipline of sound reasoning, a direct synonym for thought following rules.

clue.text: Pirate Dr Rameau streams

indicators.note: the letters of the name stream away like water and settle in a different order

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A pirate called Dr Rameau streams his content online.
explanation.walkthrough: Rameau is a French composer, which makes 'streams' sound like music online; it is the anagram indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: A pirate is a raider at sea, and one who roams looking to plunder is a marauder.

clue.text: Very large coin from yesteryear

parts.note: so = very, as in 'so good'
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A collector describes a very big coin from the old days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very large' reads as one description of the coin but splits into SO and L.
explanation.definitionFit: The sol was an old French coin, forerunner of the sou, and a former Peruvian currency unit.

clue.text: Scary hero injured when tackling Zulu warrior legend

indicators.note: a tackle wraps around its target, so the rearranged letters go around 'Zulu'
an injured thing is knocked out of shape, so 'scary hero' is rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters
Zulu is Z in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A fearsome hero is wounded while fighting a Zulu warrior of legend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Zulu warrior' looks like a unit, but Zulu is only the letter Z; the warrior belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Crazy Horse was a Lakota Sioux war leader famed for the victory at Little Bighorn.

clue.text: Vehicle packed with aged women's frosty relations

indicators.note: a vehicle packed with passengers holds them inside, so 'aged women's' goes within

parts.note: a car is a vehicle
aged = old
W is the abbreviation for women

explanation.surface: A car crammed with elderly women carries relatives who are frosty with each other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relations' seems to mean relatives in the car, but the definition is about international relations.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cold War was the long period of hostility without open fighting between the US and USSR.

clue.text: Wrong — or ill-advised — to grapple with primate

indicators.note: to grapple is to grip, so the opening words hold the answer inside them

parts.note: the letters run across 'wrong', 'or', 'ill' and 'advised'

explanation.surface: It is wrong, or at least foolish, to wrestle with a great ape.
explanation.walkthrough: The dashes and hyphen break the text into pieces, hiding the run of letters from the end of 'Wrong' to the start of 'advised'.
explanation.definitionFit: The gorilla is the largest of the great apes, which belong to the order of primates.

clue.text: Buy croquetas freshly cooked when touring northern part of Spain

indicators.note: touring means going round, so the cooked letters go round 'northern'
cooking remakes the ingredients, so 'buy croquetas' is mixed into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, twelve letters
N is the abbreviation for northern

explanation.surface: A travel tip: buy freshly fried croquetas while touring northern Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: Croquetas are Spanish fried croquettes, so the whole surface is a holiday food guide.
explanation.definitionFit: The Basque Country is an autonomous region in the north of Spain on the Bay of Biscay.

clue.text: Lear work sits 21, not the 2nd Thursday but the 1st of January

indicators.text: not the 2nd Thursday but the 1st of January
indicators.note: 'not X but Y' swaps one piece for another, here the second abbreviation for Thursday for the opening letter of January

parts.note: 21 across is UNDER THE THUMB; its 'under' is obeyed, so 'sits' goes below THE THUMB in this down entry
TH is the calendar abbreviation for Thursday; the second one in THE THUMB is dropped
the first letter of January, the '1st' the clue names
a thing that lies somewhere sits there

explanation.surface: A calendar puzzle about a work by Lear, with dates swapped from a Thursday to New Year's Day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The 2nd Thursday' and 'the 1st of January' look like dates, but they are letter instructions. In a down entry, 'sits 21' means 'sits under the thumb', so the cross-reference supplies both the letters and their position.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Lear wrote The Jumblies, the nonsense poem about folk who went to sea in a sieve.

clue.text: Ace buddy, upper-class former PM, endlessly bungling

indicators.note: something endless has lost its end, so the former prime minister's name drops its last letter

parts.note: A is ace in a pack of cards
a mate is a buddy
U is the classic label for upper-class usage
Rishi Sunak was UK prime minister from 2022 to 2024

explanation.surface: A top pal of a posh former prime minister keeps bungling things.
explanation.walkthrough: RISHI loses its final I, leaving RISH to complete A, MATE and U.
explanation.definitionFit: Amateurish work is unskilled and inept, like that of someone bungling a job.

clue.text: German economist discussing currency

indicators.note: discussing means talking about, so the currency is heard spoken rather than seen

parts.note: the mark was the German currency before the euro

explanation.surface: A German economist talks about money.
explanation.walkthrough: The Deutsche Mark makes the surface doubly German.
explanation.definitionFit: Karl Marx, born in Trier, wrote Das Kapital, the famous critique of capitalist economics.

clue.text: Wild rave with booze, which is positive

indicators.note: a wild party is out of control, so 'rave' and 'booze' are thrown into disorder

parts.note: anagram fodder
anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A wild party with plenty of drink is judged a good thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Positive' seems to be a verdict on the party but is the mathematical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A positive number is greater than nought, sitting higher than it on the number line.

clue.text: Public area former Mayor of London passed

parts.note: overt = open, public
A is the abbreviation for area
Ken Livingstone was the first elected Mayor of London

explanation.surface: An ex-Mayor of London walked through a public square.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Public area' looks like one phrase for a square, but splits into OVERT and A.
explanation.definitionFit: A car that has been passed by another on the road has been overtaken by it.

clue.text: Bare hotel, very stuffy

parts.note: Hotel is H in the NATO phonetic alphabet
a very stuffy room has no fresh air

explanation.surface: A spartan hotel room with no ventilation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bare' seems to describe the hotel's décor but defines a bald head.
explanation.definitionFit: Bare skin or a bare scalp has no covering of hair on it at all.

clue.text: The FT department regularly cancelled key private meeting

indicators.note: cancelling at regular intervals strikes out every other letter of the opening phrase

parts.note: first, third, fifth letters and so on of 'The FT department'
E is a musical key

explanation.surface: The Financial Times cancels a department's key private meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter mentions the paper that prints the puzzle. Keeping the odd letters of 'The FT department' gives all but the final E.
explanation.definitionFit: A tête-à-tête, French for head to head, is an intimate conversation between two people.

clue.text: Swear in charismatic US Senator

indicators.note: the answer is inside the following words, spanning their boundaries

parts.note: the letters run from the end of 'charismatic' into 'Senator'

explanation.definitionFit: To cuss is an informal American form of curse, meaning to use bad language.

clue.text: Cadge a generous glass

parts.note: to bum a cigarette is to cadge one
per = a, as in 'ten pounds a head'

explanation.surface: Someone scrounges a large drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a' looks like a mere article but gives PER.

clue.text: Oppressed in the digital sphere?

parts.note: surface reading: people downtrodden in the online world of computers; setter's reading: digital means to do with the digits, the fingers, so the oppression is beneath one of them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Digital' suggests technology, but a digit is also a finger, and the idiom for being dominated puts you beneath one.
explanation.definitionFit: Being dominated or controlled by someone is the idiom, pressed down by a finger.

clue.text: Greeting husband plucking wings of chicken

indicators.note: plucking a bird's wings pulls off its sides, so the word for 'chicken' loses its outer letters

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for husband
chicken and yellow both mean cowardly

explanation.walkthrough: 'Chicken' looks like the bird being plucked, but means cowardly, which is YELLOW; losing its Y and W leaves ELLO.
explanation.definitionFit: Hello is the everyday word spoken when meeting someone or answering a phone.

clue.text: Hugh and Glyn when undressed not much to look at

indicators.note: undressing strips off the outer layer, so both names lose their first and last letters

parts.note: the inside of 'Hugh'
the inside of 'Glyn'

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the verdict on the naked men is also the answer.

clue.text: His nibs can occasionally be found in here

definitions.text: His nibs can occasionally be found in here

parts.note: surface reading: 'his nibs' is a mocking name for a self-important man, the boss who sometimes turns up here; setter's reading: the nibs are the metal points of a man's pens, dipped now and then into a pot at the desk

clue.text: Contents of penniless family members

explanation.definitionFit: Kin are relatives, the people related to you by blood.

the Indian Premier League, the Twenty20 cricket competition held in India

explanation.definitionFit: Winning with ease, without any effort or doubt, is the idiom from horse racing.

clue.text: Dull, well-behaved prisoner getting time off
